title: The AI Megawatt Is Not a Megawatt
seoTitle: What 1 GW of AI Data Center Power Actually Means
subtitle: How grid, facility, and IT power translate into installed GPUs—and where the conversion stops.
seoDescription: A current GB300 model translating a 1 GW data-center claim across grid interconnection, facility power, PUE, network overhead, rack capacity, installed GPUs, and utilization.

artwork.label: Grid / facility / compute
artwork.note: A capacity ladder from electrical boundary to installed and utilized accelerators.

author: SULAYMAN BOWLES
thesis: A gigawatt converts into a GPU fleet only after its electrical boundary, status, and time basis are known.

conclusion.title: Read the boundary first
conclusion.content: A 1 GW facility supports about 402,574 installed B300 GPUs in this reference design, with 355,819–434,856 across engineering sensitivities. A grid request alone supports no fleet estimate. Establish what the gigawatt measures before using it to compare capacity, costs, or output.

evidenceBoundary: This is a homogeneous GB300 reference conversion, not a forecast of any named data center. The 142 kW rack value is an “up to” specification; PUE and external-IT factors are scenarios; the 50% interconnection-utilization example is illustrative; network power is incomplete beyond the documented eight-SU design; computational utilization does not equal useful work or revenue utilization.

content: A “1 GW” AI data center does not identify a GPU fleet. The figure may describe a grid request, facility capacity, IT capacity, or average draw. Each has a different meaning.

For a 1,000 MW facility using homogeneous GB300 NVL72 racks, PUE 1.145, and 10% external IT overhead, the model supports 402,574 installed B300 GPUs. That is a conditional engineering estimate, not a universal conversion. Change the electrical boundary and the answer changes; disclose only a grid request and the fleet remains unknown.

sections.title: What the gigawatt measures
paragraphs: Utility filings, construction announcements, and hardware plans use the same unit for different quantities. A grid request concerns the connection point. Facility nameplate includes cooling, power conversion, lighting, and other infrastructure. IT nameplate excludes that layer; rack nameplate excludes much of the network, storage, and control plane. Average demand measures a time-weighted flow.

LBNL warns that annual energy, average and maximum demand, facility nameplate, and requested interconnection capacity cannot be converted reliably without project-specific relationships. Its grid definition includes total facility needs and design margins. It estimates interconnection utilization around 50% because of redundancy and maintenance, but says the value is poorly documented. Use it as an illustration, not a general ratio. [S8]

Before converting, establish boundary, status, and time basis. Announced, requested, firm, energized, commissioned, and occupied capacity describe different states. Phasing and reserved space or power can leave the installed fleet smaller than the headline suggests.

sections.title: Follow the power
paragraphs: The reference case starts with 1,000 MW of total facility nameplate. This controlled boundary allows PUE to be applied once; it does not describe how most announcements are written.

It assumes homogeneous GB300 NVL72 racks. Real campuses mix accelerators, CPUs, storage, network generations, development clusters, spares, and partially occupied halls. Holding hardware constant isolates the boundary problem; it does not forecast a company’s asset register.

Divide facility MW by PUE to obtain IT MW. Reserve external IT power for scale-out networking, storage, support servers, and management. Convert the remainder into racks and GPUs using NVIDIA’s rack specification. Every output depends on those inputs.

table.caption: Reference formulas and units
rows: Rack MW = IT MW ÷ (1 + external IT overhead)

sections.title: Use the whole rack
paragraphs: NVIDIA’s reference architecture defines one GB300 NVL72 scalable unit as a liquid-cooled rack: 18 compute trays, 72 B300 GPUs, and 36 Grace CPUs, requiring up to 142 kW. Each tray also contains ConnectX-8 adapters, a BlueField DPU, boot storage, and local cache, alongside four GPUs and two CPUs. [S1][S2]

Dividing a gigawatt by per-GPU thermal design power omits CPUs, memory, NVLink, storage, adapters, management hardware, and conversion losses inside the cabinet. This model starts with rack power because that boundary includes them.
“Up to 142 kW” is a maximum requirement, not continuous draw. It gives a conservative rack count at fixed compute-rack nameplate. Annual energy requires a separate utilization model.

sections.title: Account for the network
paragraphs: NVIDIA’s eight-SU bill of materials specifies eight racks, 576 GPUs, 44 compute-core switches, 11 converged-core switches, and 16 OOB management switches. Using SN5600 passive-cable typical power plus SN2201 power gives 53.27 kW: 4.69% of the racks’ combined 1.136 MW nameplate, before storage, support servers, customer-edge equipment, or additional network tiers. [S3][S6][S7]

The documents disagree on hardware. The BOM and logical architecture name SN5600; the networking-hardware page names SN5610. Its specification gives 900 W with passive cables and 2.08 kW with 64 optical modules. Applying the optical figure to 55 high-speed switches raises the comparator to 115.97 kW, or 10.21% of rack nameplate. This is an optics comparison, not an assumption that every port is populated. [S3][S5][S6]

An eight-rack design cannot be scaled by simple multiplication. NVIDIA separates fabrics in larger designs and introduces a super-spine around 1,024 nodes. Storage, customer, support-server, and management networks also sit outside the compute fabric. The reference fleet has roughly 100,000 compute trays, far beyond the documented design point. [S4]

The model therefore tests external IT overhead of 6%, 10%, and 14%. Six percent sits above the passive-switch floor; ten percent approaches the optics comparator before unquantified support equipment. Fourteen percent comes from a GB200-era Epoch total-IT/server decomposition: a magnitude check, not a GB300 measurement. [S9]

sections.title: Convert facility power into GPUs
paragraphs: LBNL estimates average PUE of 1.145 for facilities serving AI equipment in 2024. PUE divides total facility energy by IT energy. Applied to the reference case, 1,000 MW ÷ 1.145 leaves 873.36 MW for IT. A 10% external IT allowance, measured on top of compute-rack power, leaves 793.97 MW for GB300 racks. At 142 kW and 72 GPUs per rack, that supports 5,591.31 rack equivalents and 402,574 installed B300 GPUs. [S1][S8]

PUE 1.10 with 6% external IT overhead yields 434,856 GPUs; PUE 1.25 with 14% yields 355,819. These are engineering sensitivities, not confidence bounds. The 79,037-GPU difference equals about 1,098 GB300 racks.
The boundary error can be larger still: treating a grid request as IT capacity, or applying PUE to an IT number that already excludes facility overhead.

sections.title: Change the boundary, change the answer
paragraphs: Epoch’s one-gigawatt cost model starts with IT nameplate and applies PUE and utilization separately for operating energy. At that boundary, a 10% external IT allowance leaves 909.09 MW for racks and supports 460,948 B300 GPUs—roughly 58,000 more than the facility reference, because facility overhead sits outside the gigawatt. [S10]

A 1 GW grid request gives no fleet estimate. LBNL’s illustrative 50% average utilization implies 500 MW of average facility draw and 4.38 TWh per year. It reveals neither facility nameplate—1 GW, 700 MW, 500 MW, or phased halls—nor PUE, external IT share, rack density, or occupancy. [S8]

Time also changes the claim. Epoch’s Frontier Data Centers Hub notes that campuses open in stages and companies may not clarify incremental timelines. Announced, under-construction, energized, commissioned, and occupied capacity remain separate states. [S11]

sections.title: Installed capacity is not output
paragraphs: Keeping 402,574 B300 GPUs powered on for a year yields 3.53 billion powered-on GPU-hours. That counts time, not computational work.

LBNL defines utilization as average computational intensity relative to maximum. It assumes 80% for training, with a 75%–85% range, and 20% for inference by 2030, with a 30% high-inference case. The reference fleet yields 2.64–3.00 billion training full-load-equivalent GPU-hours, 0.705 billion at 20% inference utilization, and 1.06 billion at 30%. [S8]

These hours still omit architecture, precision, sparsity, communication, checkpointing, failed jobs, software quality, throttling, and hardware-generation differences. They separate installed capacity from annual intensity; they do not measure useful work.

Nor do they measure revenue. Paid utilization depends on reservations, service obligations, internal workloads, customer mix, pricing, credits, and spare capacity needed for peaks. Engineering documentation does not establish those economics.

sections.title: What a capacity claim should disclose
paragraphs: A reconstructable claim starts with electrical boundary, status, and time, then states hardware, facility, and utilization assumptions. Unknowns and ranges are acceptable. Combining requested power, energized power, installed IT, and active compute into one figure is not.

For investors, these distinctions affect capex intensity, commissioning risk, revenue timing, depreciation, and utilization. For utilities, they affect load forecasts and reserves. For operators, they locate the constraint: interconnection, mechanical plant, white space, power delivery, networking, storage, or scheduling.
bullets: Boundary: interconnection, facility, IT, rack, or average draw.
Status: announced, requested, firm, energized, commissioned, occupied, or active.
Time basis: current, phase date, full-build date, peak, or annual average.
Redundancy and margin: what is reserved and why.
PUE: value, period, load point, and measurement boundary.
IT allocation: server/rack, network, storage, support, and management shares.
Hardware: accelerator generation, rack architecture, quantity, and mix.
Utilization: computational, electrical, scheduling, and paid utilization kept separate.
Staging: phase-by-phase energized and occupied capacity.
Source: utility filing, one-line, vendor order, asset register, or management estimate.

sections.title: Limits of the model
paragraphs: This is not a campus forecast. Firm interconnection, topology, PUE curve, cooling, storage, port population, spares, power caps, rack loading, accelerator mix, occupancy, workloads, and bookings remain unknown.

A site may fit more racks if average or capped draw is lower, provided its electrical and thermal design supports that policy. Redundancy, stranded capacity, maintenance, or topology may instead prevent full occupancy. Nameplate arithmetic does not resolve either case.

The external IT range is not measured at gigawatt scale. It draws on an eight-SU switch reconstruction, an optics comparator, architectural requirements, and a GB200-era magnitude check. Storage and support infrastructure remain unquantified.

A GPU is not a stable performance unit across generations, precisions, models, software, or workloads. The model reports physical B300 units and B300 GPU-hours; it does not infer H100-equivalents, FLOP/s, tokens, training runs, or revenue.
